rationale: The book's core identification—that erga nomou names deeds considered in relation to law, without fixing one unchanging class of deeds or equating them with obedience, while consistently denying their capacity to purchase justification, the Spirit, covenant standing, or place God in debt—accounts for the full set of occurrences and surrounding arguments better than any fixed-class alternative. It unifies the texts that explicitly name God's law (Rom 3:20, 28; Gal 3:10; Rom 9:32 TR) with the circumcision-party contexts (Gal 2:16) and the unnamed-act contrasts (Gal 3:2, 5) without forcing Paul into self-contradiction on the goodness of the law, the establishment of the law by faith, or the requirement of good works as the fruit of grace. The strongest fixed-class counters each leave residual texts unexplained or require secondary flattening of Paul's named distinctions among laws and of his explicit rejection of the wage-debt claim.
book_core_identification: Works of the law are deeds considered in relation to law (context identifies the particular acts or application); the phrase is not a synonym for obedience and does not identify one unchanging class of deeds; what remains constant is the rejected claim made for those deeds (they cannot purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt).
book_secondary_elaborations: Distinction between a work (deed) and obedience (relation of the deed to a legitimate command), so that the same outward act can be either depending on the claim made for it
Classification of specific occurrences (Rom 3 = God's law; Gal 2 = circumcision-party application; Gal 3:2/5 = ambiguous/unnamed; Gal 3:10 = God's law; Rom 9:32 TR = God's law)
Integration with the telos reading of Christ as the goal/purpose of the law rather than its termination
Rejection of both pure abolition and pure legalism readings via Paul's named laws (law of God vs. law of sin, etc.) and the wage-debt picture of Romans 4

Contextual handling of parallel phrases (not of works, not under the law, curse of the law, schoolmaster, letter vs. spirit, ordinances) as dominion, debt-cancellation, or administration changes rather than wholesale repeal of God's standard
strongest_counter_interpretation: The traditional Protestant/Reformation reading (dominant popular and still widely taught): 'works of the law' (erga nomou) denotes deeds of obedience to the Mosaic law, understood as any human effort, moral or ritual performance, or law-keeping undertaken to earn or establish righteousness before God; the phrase functions as the negative pole of the faith-versus-works contrast, symbolizing legalism, self-reliant achievement, and works-righteousness opposed to justification by grace through faith alone.
counter_core_identification: Works of the law = human deeds of Mosaic-law obedience (or more broadly any meritorious effort) offered as the basis for justification; they are categorically excluded as the means of righteousness, in contrast to faith.
material_core_denial: The counter treats the phrase as naming one relatively fixed class of deeds (law-keeping / human merit-effort) whose very performance or reliance is the problem, rather than deeds whose identity is supplied by context while the constant error is the purchase-price claim made for them; it therefore collapses the work/obedience distinction and cannot comfortably accommodate Paul's simultaneous affirmation that the law is holy, is established by faith, is fulfilled by love/Spirit-walking, and that believers are created for good works.
counter_case: Surface contrast in the core texts: 'not justified by works of the law but through faith' (Gal 2:16; Rom 3:20, 28) appears to set two mutually exclusive instruments of justification against each other
Gal 3:10 places those 'of the works of the law' under the Deuteronomic curse for incomplete performance, suggesting the problem is reliance on doing the law
Rom 9:32 (and broader Abraham/Rom 4 parallels) frames Israel's failure as pursuing righteousness 'as it were by works' rather than by faith
Broader Pauline 'not of works' statements (Eph 2:8-9; Titus 3:5; Rom 4:4-5 wage-debt picture) are commonly read as synonymous, extending the exclusion to any human achievement
Historical Reformation usage solidified the legalism-versus-grace polarity as the controlling frame
book_explanatory_advantages: Handles both clear God's-law texts (Rom 3; Gal 3:10) and circumcision-party/boundary texts (Gal 2) under one principle without special pleading or redefinition of nomos

Preserves Paul's explicit affirmations that the law is holy/spiritual/good, that faith establishes the law (Rom 3:31), that the Spirit fulfills the righteous requirement of the law (Rom 8:4), and that love fulfills the law (Gal 5:14; Rom 13:10)
Explains why Paul can circumcise Timothy, keep feast days, and demonstrate orderly law-keeping while still condemning the Galatian demand for circumcision as justification gate
Unifies the wage-debt picture of Rom 4 and Luke 17:10 with the positive command of good works (Eph 2:10; Titus 3:8) without contradiction
Accounts for the textual variation in Rom 9:32 (TR 'works of the law' vs. critical 'by works') by focusing on manner/claim rather than a fixed code of deeds
counter_explanatory_advantages: Matches the immediate rhetorical polarity of faith vs. works-of-law in the justification texts and the popular 'not of works' summary
Provides a simple, memorable pastoral contrast against self-reliant religion that has shaped centuries of Protestant preaching
Aligns with the surface reading of Gal 3:10's curse on incomplete doers and the Abraham example of faith credited rather than wages earned
decisive_sources: Romans 3:20, 28, 31 (law gives knowledge of sin yet is established by faith)
Galatians 2:16 in its immediate Antioch/circumcision context (Gal 2:11-14)
Galatians 3:10 quoting Deuteronomy 27:26 (explicit 'book of the law') together with Gal 3:13 (curse, not the law itself, is removed)
Galatians 3:2, 5 (Spirit by hearing of faith, no act named)
Romans 4:4-5 (work as wage/debt claim) + Luke 17:10 (even perfect obedience creates no surplus)
1 Corinthians 7:19 (circumcision nothing; keeping commandments of God is what matters)
Romans 7:12, 14, 22; 8:3-4 (law holy/spiritual; Spirit fulfills its righteousness)
Ephesians 2:8-10 (not of works, yet created unto good works)
unresolved_objections: The traditional reading remains the more intuitive first-pass gloss of the faith-versus-works polarity for many readers and preachers; the book's more precise claim-based reading requires sustained attention to context and cross-references

Whether every Second-Temple hearer would have heard the phrase with the same flexibility the book proposes remains historically underdetermined (4QMMT and NPP data still invite debate on boundary-marker prominence)
The exact scope of 'ordinances' in Eph 2:15 and the debt-record in Col 2:14 continues to admit alternative construals even under the book's framework
